messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sami, a 40-year-old Middle Eastern man and paramedic, has been struggling with his mental health ever since he witnessed a traumatic event at work where he failed to save a loved one. The incident occurred during a chaotic scene in a hospital emergency room filled with the antiseptic smell that now triggers intense anxiety for him. He recalls the sight of visible injuries and wounds on others, which only intensify the trauma. Sami’s wife has noticed a significant change in his behavior over the past few months. What frightens her most is when he reacts with alarm to unexpected touches, even from her. His difficulty concentrating at work has led to multiple errors, causing him immense distress. The trauma has left him feeling permanently changed for the worse and questioning his ability to rely on himself. One of Sami’s coping mechanisms involves trying hard not to think about the traumatic event. He suppresses thoughts that come up involuntarily, but this only leads to a cycle where the memories feel completely real when they do surface, reliving all the terror he experienced at the time. This full sensory reliving often happens unpredictably and leaves him feeling helpless and haunted by his failure to protect others. Sami’s constant need to feel safe has made work particularly challenging. He always chooses the safest seat in a vehicle or room, which only highlights how much the trauma has altered his sense of security. The thought that he can’t rely on himself further exacerbates this fear, as he often finds himself hyper-vigilant and startled by even minor events. His efforts to suppress thoughts about the event have led him to overwork at his paramedic job. By throwing himself into tasks, Sami hopes to keep his mind occupied, but this behavior only perpetuates his symptoms. The memories of that day still flood back vividly during moments when he’s overwhelmed by triggers like the antiseptic smell or seeing injured patients. These intense recollections often leave him with memory gaps, where parts of the event remain unclear, adding to his sense of helplessness and guilt. Sami has started avoiding work altogether on days when he feels particularly anxious about encountering these triggers. This avoidance behavior, however, only reinforces his belief that he can’t rely on himself in critical situations, deepening his negative appraisals and making him more vulnerable to further anxiety. His wife’s concern over his deteriorating mental health finally pushed Sami to seek help. What frightens him most is the fear of never recovering from this trauma and becoming permanently damaged. He hopes that with professional support, he can find a way to cope more effectively without feeling like he has failed himself or others again. In therapy sessions, Sami expresses his deepest fears about being forever changed by what happened. These negative appraisals drive much of his behavior and make it challenging for him to feel secure in any environment. His hyper-vigilance and startled reactions only serve to reinforce these beliefs, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that he finds increasingly difficult to break. The memory gaps about the traumatic event further contribute to Sami’s sense of unreliability. He often wonders what parts of the event he has forgotten, which adds to his overall distress and belief in his own failure as a paramedic and protector. These memories, when they do emerge, are so vivid that they feel entirely real, amplifying his fear and reinforcing the cycle of negative appraisals. Sami’s overworking is both a coping mechanism and a manifestation of his guilt. By pushing himself to work harder, he hopes to compensate for what he sees as his failure in protecting others. However, this strategy only leads to more errors at work due to difficulty concentrating, further validating his belief that he can’t rely on himself. Sami’s current state is one of intense anxiety and fear about the future. He has come to believe that he is permanently damaged by what happened and that he will never fully recover. What he most hopes for is a way out of this cycle of trauma and a return to feeling like he can trust himself again.
